La [[fn-derivadas|derivada]] entra en el: The [[fn-derivadas|derivative]] enters the shader the way it is computed in practice: by subtracting neighbours, just as in [[av-numerico|numerical analysis]], with the step fixed at one pixel. With it the soft edge measures itself, and a height field turns into relief lit with a [[ge-vectores|dot product]].
Hasta ahora hemos puesto los bordes suav: So far we have set the soft edges by hand: smoothstep(0.0, 0.02, d), and that 0.02 came out of trying until it looked right. It works at one size and fails at every other. If you zoom in, the edge becomes a cloud; if you move away, it goes back to being a staircase. This topic fixes that once and for all, and along the way puts the [[fn-derivadas|derivative]] inside the shader.
El píxel sí sabe algo de sus vecinos: The pixel does know something about its neighbours
Te dije al principio que cada píxel se c: I told you at the start that each pixel computes itself alone, knowing nothing about the others. It was almost true. The graphics card does not process the pixels one at a time: it groups them into little two-by-two quads and runs the same program for all four at once, step by step. That means that, at any point of the program, a pixel can ask what a variable is at the pixel next door, because its quad-mate is on exactly the same line.
De ahí salen tres funciones:: Out of that come three functions:
cuánto cambia <code>v</code> al moverse: how much v changes on moving one pixel to the right
how much v changes on moving one pixel upwards
<code>abs(dFdx(v)) + abs(dFdy(v))</code>: abs(dFdx(v)) + abs(dFdy(v)): how much it changes in total on moving one pixel diagonally
Eso es una <strong>derivada</strong>, y: That is a derivative, and it is exactly the one you studied in [[fn-derivadas|derivatives]], but computed the way it is computed in practice and not on paper: by finite differences, subtracting two neighbouring values, with no limit and no algebra. It is the same method as the [[av-numerico|numerical analysis]] topic's, with the unusual advantage that here the step $h$ is exactly one pixel and there is no need to choose it.
Y como <code>v</code> puede ser cualquie: And since v can be anything —a coordinate, a distance, a colour— what you are differentiating is your own program, without having written it anywhere. The card does not know what formula you used: it just subtracts.
El precio de esa magia es que la respues: The price of that magic is that the answer is the same for all four pixels of the quad, so the derivatives have a resolution of two pixels, not one. And there is a rule that bites: do not call dFdx inside an if that some pixels of the quad enter and others do not. If a quad-mate never reached that line, there is nothing to subtract and the result is rubbish.
Ahora el arreglo. Si <code>d</code> es l: Now the fix. If d is the signed distance to the figure, fwidth(d) tells you how much distance there is in one pixel. And that is exactly the width the transition must have to take up one pixel and not one more:

Un relieve a partir de un número: A relief out of a number
La segunda cosa que abren las derivadas: The second thing the derivatives open up is more spectacular. Take any function giving a number per point —the previous topic's noise, for instance— and treat it as a height map: where it is large, there is a mountain. Its [[av-vectorial|gradient]] points uphill, and with it you can manufacture the surface's normal, which is the direction each little patch of terrain faces.
Y con la normal se ilumina: cuanto más d: And with the normal you light: the more squarely a patch faces the light, the brighter it shines. That dot product between the normal and the light's direction is all the diffuse lighting you need, and it is the same [[ge-vectores|dot product]] as in the geometry of the plane.
El mismo fbm de nubes del tema anterior,: The same cloud fbm as the previous topic, but now read as height and lit with a turning light. It stops looking like a patch and starts looking like terrain.
Con relieve 0,1 el terreno es casi plano: With relief 0.1 the terrain is almost flat. Will the light's turning show more with high or low relief? Which component of the normal dominates when the relief is low?
Un relieve rocoso generado por ruido, il: A rocky relief generated by noise, lit by a light turning around it.
Ese <code>iResolution.y * 0.02</code> es: That iResolution.y * 0.02 is only a scale factor: it converts “how much the height changes per pixel” into something comparable with the 1 of the third component. Raise it and the terrain becomes craggy; lower it and it flattens.
Este truco se llama <em>bump mapping</em: This trick is called bump mapping and it is a beautiful lie: the surface is as flat as a board, there is not a single bump anywhere. The only thing that has changed is which way each point says it faces, and the eye swallows the whole relief. If you look at the figure's edge, the lie collapses: it is still straight.
Restar el valor de un vecino al de otro: Subtracting one neighbour's value from another's is applying a kernel of three numbers, $(-1, 0, 1)$: it is [[av-convolucion|a convolution]] with the smallest kernel that detects changes. And if instead of choosing those three numbers by hand you let them be learned from examples, out comes the first layer of [[ia-cnn|a convolutional network]], whose filters end up looking very much like this one.
Estos tres números también se pueden apr: These three numbers can also be learned
Las derivadas del hardware están detrás: The hardware's derivatives lie behind three things you see constantly. The first, the antialiasing of the edges in any modern interface. The second, bump mapping: the roughness of almost every surface in a video game is this. And the third, invisible: when a texture is seen from far away, the card uses fwidth to decide which reduced version of the image to take, and that is why distant roads do not shimmer.
El truco del relieve falso lo publicó Ja: The fake relief trick was published by James Blinn in 1978, and its elegance lies in realising that the eye does not judge a surface's shape by its silhouette but by how it shares out the light. Ten years later, cards started grouping pixels into two-by-two quads for reasons of efficiency, with no thought of derivatives, and somebody realised that that engineering decision was giving away a differential operator for free.
